common_name: Fireball Bee Balm (Compact Mildew-Resistant Ruby-Red Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Fireball is a compact, mounding bee balm bred for tight round heads of ruby-red flowers on a plant far smaller than heirloom Monarda didyma cultivars.

directions: Plant in average to consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to keep foliage dry and airy. Fireball is a dwarf, patented selection of scarlet bee balm bred to hold a tight, mounding shape well under two feet tall, so it stays upright in the front of a border without staking or flopping the way many tall heirloom Monarda didyma cultivars do by midsummer. The dense clusters of tubular ruby-red flowers open from tidy round buds from midsummer into early fall and are a strong draw for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies. Bred with improved resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures most bee balm foliage in humid climates, it still benefits from good air circulation and division of congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor and airflow.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Perennial Bee Balm Cultivars

common_name: Croftway Pink Bee Balm (Heirloom Clear Rose-Pink Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; introduced in 1932, Croftway Pink is a long-cultivated heirloom bee balm that will not come true from seed and should be propagated by division.

directions: Plant in average to moist, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Introduced in 1932, Croftway Pink is one of the longest-cultivated Monarda didyma cultivars still widely grown, valued for clear, soft rose-pink flowers held in terminal whorls above aromatic, lance-shaped leaves, and for notably good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many older red and purple bee balm selections. Like other bergamots it spreads by shallow rhizomes to form an expanding colony over time and is a strong magnet for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies through its long midsummer bloom season. Divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to renew vigor, improve air circulation, and keep the planting within bounds.

common_name: Leading Lady Plum Bee Balm (Extra-Compact Early-Blooming Mildew-Resistant Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Leading Lady Plum is an extremely compact, densely branched hybrid that begins flowering earlier in the season than most bee balm.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Leading Lady Plum is a dwarf, densely branched bee balm hybrid bred to stay under fifteen inches tall while spreading wider than it is tall, forming a tidy mounded plant that needs no staking and suits the front of a border or a large container. Magenta-purple flowers with near-black bracts and a fine dusting of dark purple spots open earlier in the season than most bee balm cultivars and continue from early into midsummer, drawing bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. It was bred for exceptional resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures most Monarda foliage, but still benefits from even moisture and good air movement between plants. Deadhead spent flower heads to tidy the plant and divide congested clumps every few years in early spring.

common_name: Athens Blue Spires Rosemary (Extra Cold-Hardy Upright Georgia Gem Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Athens Blue Spires was selected at the University of Georgia trial gardens for extensively self-branching upright growth and exceptional cold hardiness among rosemary cultivars.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Athens Blue Spires was selected at the University of Georgia Horticulture Department trial gardens in Athens as one of Allen Armitage's Georgia Gems, chosen for an upright, extensively self-branching habit, extremely narrow needle-like leaves, and light blue flowers produced heavily from winter into spring. It is among the most cold-hardy rosemary selections available, tolerating winter lows well below what damages standard culinary rosemary, which makes it a reliable choice for gardeners at the cooler edge of rosemary's range. Prune after the main flowering flush to maintain a dense, upright form, and avoid heavy or poorly drained soil, which threatens rosemary far more than cold does in most gardens.

common_name: Corsican Blue Rosemary (Vigorous Semi-Prostrate Deep-Blue-Flowered Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained sandy soil in full sun; Corsican Blue is a vigorous, semi-prostrate rosemary with narrow dark leaves, grown as much for its strongly aromatic foliage as for its deep blue flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun. Corsican Blue is a dense, semi-prostrate rosemary selection, part of the narrow-leaved Angustifolia Group, prized as one of the most intensely aromatic rosemary cultivars available along with small tubular deep blue flowers borne over a long spring-into-summer season. Its sprawling, cascading habit suits raised beds, banks, and the tops of retaining walls where the stems can spill downward, and the finely textured, dark green needle-like foliage remains ornamental year-round in mild climates. Harvest sprigs regularly for cooking to keep growth dense, and site in sharply drained soil, since wet feet are the most common cause of failure.

common_name: Doretta Klaber Thyme (Tight Miniature Mat-Forming Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Doretta Klaber is one of the tightest-growing thyme cultivars, forming a ground-hugging hummock barely two inches tall.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun. Doretta Klaber is a miniature thyme cultivar with minute, fuzzy gray-green leaves that form an exceptionally tight, ground-hugging mat, among the tightest-growing forms in the genus, so dense that few weeds can compete once it is established. Tufts of deep lavender-pink flowers cover the mat in early summer, and the foliage takes on mahogany tones in cold weather for extra seasonal interest. Its diminutive scale suits troughs, stone walls, staircases, and the cracks between paving stones far better than open groundcover use. Shear lightly after bloom to keep growth dense, and avoid heavy or wet soil, which quickly rots the shallow roots.

common_name: Purple Carpet Creeping Thyme (Dense Mat-Forming Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Purple Carpet is a fast-spreading, low-growing creeping thyme suited to pathways, rock gardens, and stepping-stone joints.

directions: Plant in average to dry, sharply drained soil in full sun to part shade. Purple Carpet forms a fast-growing, dense, low mat of tiny aromatic leaves that stays under three inches tall and knits together quickly to make an attractive, walkable groundcover between stepping stones or along the edge of a path. Masses of small rose-purple flowers cover the foliage in early summer and are a strong draw for bees. It dislikes excessive moisture and poor drainage far more than it dislikes drought or foot traffic, and tends to decline in heavy clay or wet winter soil. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and encourage fresh growth for the following season.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Thyme Cultivar Notes

common_name: Snowdrift Creeping Thyme (White-Flowered Mat-Forming Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, free-draining soil in full sun; Snowdrift is a mat-forming creeping thyme grown for its clusters of pure white summer flowers rather than the pink or purple tones typical of the species.

directions: Plant in moist but sharply draining soil in full sun. Snowdrift is a low, evergreen, mat-forming thyme selection with small dark green leaves and dense clusters of pure white flowers in summer, giving it a cooler, brighter effect in the garden than the more common pink- and purple-flowered creeping thymes. It is well suited to rock gardens, gravel paths, and the joints between paving stones, where its flat habit tolerates light foot traffic once established. Bees visit the flowers readily. Like other creeping thymes it resents wet, poorly drained soil and heavy shade; shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy.

common_name: Buckland Ornamental Oregano (Dusty Pink Hop-Flowered Trailing Oregano)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Buckland is a low, spreading ornamental oregano grown for its dusty-pink, hop-like flower bracts rather than for culinary use.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade. Buckland is a low, spreading ornamental oregano with small, rounded, blue-green aromatic leaves, blooming all summer with whorls of pendulous, dusty-pink, hop-like bracts that half-conceal tiny orchid-pink flowers, giving it a softer, more subdued look than brighter hop-flowered oreganos. The foliage is aromatic but not grown for the kitchen, since flavor and oil content are much lower than culinary Greek oregano. It works well trailing over the front of a sunny border, in containers, hanging baskets, or window boxes, and the persistent flower bracts can be cut for dried arrangements. Shear lightly after the main flowering flush to keep growth compact and encourage rebloom.
